[[File:Lissajous toric knot 5 6 22.png|thumb|300px|Lissajous-toric knot with parameters 5, 6 and 22 in braid form (with z-axis in horizontal direction)]]
In [[knot theory]], a '''Lissajous-toric knot''' is a [[knot (mathematics)|knot]] defined by [[parametric equations]] of the form:

<math>x(t)=(2+\sin qt)\cos Nt, \qquad y(t)=(2+\sin qt)\sin Nt, \qquad z(t)=\cos p(t+\phi),</math>

where <math>N</math>, <math>p</math>, and <math>q</math> are [[integer]]s, the [[phase shift]] <math>\phi</math> is a [[real number]]
and the parameter <math>t</math> varies between 0 and <math>2\pi</math>.<ref>See M. Soret and M. Ville: Lissajous-toric knots, 
J. Knot Theory Ramifications 29, 2050003 (2020).</ref>

For <math>p=q</math> the knot is a [[torus knot]].

== Braid and billiard knot definitions ==
[[File:Lissajous-toric-knot T 4 7 35.png|thumb|200px|Lissajous-toric knot T(4,7,35) as a billiard knot, showing period 7]]
In [[braid group|braid]] form these knots can be defined in a square solid torus (i.e. the cube <math>[-1,1]^3</math> with identified top and bottom) as

:<math>x(t)=\sin 2\pi qt, \qquad y(t)=\cos 2\pi p(t+\phi), \qquad z(t)=2(N t - \lfloor N t\rfloor )-1, \qquad t \in [0,1]</math>.

The projection of this Lissajous-toric knot onto the x-y-plane is a [[Lissajous curve]].

Replacing the sine and cosine functions in the parametrization by a [[triangle wave]] transforms a Lissajous-toric
knot isotopically into a billiard curve inside the solid torus. Because of this property Lissajous-toric knots are also called billiard knots in a solid torus.<ref>See C. Lamm: 
Deformation of cylinder knots, 4th chapter of Ph.D. thesis, ‘Zylinder-Knoten und symmetrische Vereinigungen‘, Bonner Mathematische Schriften 321 (1999), available since 2012 as {{arXiv|1210.6639}}.</ref>

Lissajous-toric knots were first studied as billiard knots and they share many properties with billiard knots in a cylinder.<ref>See C. Lamm and 
D. Obermeyer: Billiard knots in a cylinder, J. Knot Theory Ramifications 8, 353–-366 (1999).</ref>
They also occur in the analysis of singularities of [[minimal surface]]s with branch points<ref>See Soret/Ville.</ref> and in the study of 
the [[Three-body problem]].<ref>See E. Kin, H. Nakamura and H. Ogawa: Lissajous 3-braids, J. Math. Soc. Japan 75, 195--228 (2023) (or {{arXiv|2008.00585v4}}).</ref>

The knots in the subfamily with <math>p = q \cdot l</math>, with an integer <math>l \ge 1</math>, are known as ′Lemniscate knots′.<ref>See B. Bode, M.R. Dennis, 
D. Foster and R.P. King: [https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rspa.2016.0829 Knotted fields and explicit fibrations for lemniscate knots], 
Proc. Royal Soc. A (2017).</ref> Lemniscate knots have period <math>q</math> and are [[Fibered knot|fibred]]. The knot shown on the right is of this type (with <math>l=5</math>).

== Properties ==
[[File:Lissajous-toric knot T 3 8 7.svg|thumb|400px|Symmetries of the Lissajous-toric knot T(3,8,7): symmetric union (vertical axis), rotation into mirror image and palindromic property within Q (horizontal axis)]]
Lissajous-toric knots are denoted by <math>K(N,q,p,\phi)</math>. To ensure that the knot is traversed only once in the parametrization 
the conditions <math>\gcd(N,q)=\gcd(N,p)=1</math> are needed. In addition, singular values for the phase, leading to self-intersections, have to be excluded.

The isotopy class of Lissajous-toric knots surprisingly does not depend on the phase <math>\phi</math> (up to mirroring). 
If the distinction between a knot and its mirror image is not important, the notation <math>K(N,q,p)</math> can be used.

The properties of Lissajous-toric knots depend on whether <math>p</math> and <math>q</math> are coprime or <math>d=\gcd(p,q)>1</math>. The main properties are:
* Interchanging <math>p</math> and <math>q</math>:
:<math>K(N,q,p)=K(N,p,q)</math> (up to mirroring).
* Ribbon property:
:If <math>p</math> and <math>q</math> are coprime, <math>K(N,q,p)</math> is a symmetric union and therefore a [[ribbon knot]].
* Periodicity: 
:If <math>d=\gcd(p,q)>1</math>, the Lissajous-toric knot has period <math>d</math> and the factor knot is a ribbon knot.
* Strongly positive amphicheirality:
:If <math>p</math> and <math>q</math> have different parity, then <math>K(N,q,p)</math> is strongly positive amphicheiral.
* Period 2: 
:If <math>p</math> and <math>q</math> are both odd, then <math>K(N,q,p)</math> has period 2 (for even <math>N</math>) or is freely 2-periodic (for odd <math>N</math>).

=== Example ===
The knot T(3,8,7), shown in the graphics, is a symmetric union and a ribbon knot (in fact, it is the composite knot  <math>5_1 \sharp -5_1</math>).
It is strongly positive amphicheiral: a rotation by <math>\pi</math> maps the knot to its mirror image, keeping its orientation.
An additional horizontal symmetry occurs as a combination of the vertical symmetry and the rotation (′double palindromicity′ in Kin/Nakamura/Ogawa).

== ′Classification′ of billiard rooms ==
In the following table a systematic overview of the possibilities to build billiard rooms from the interval and the circle (interval with identified boundaries) is given:
{| class="wikitable"
|-
! Billiard room || Billiard knots 
|-
| <math>[-1,1]^3</math> || [[Lissajous knot]]s
|-
| <math>[-1,1]^2 \times \mathbb{S}^1</math> || Lissajous-toric knots
|-
| <math>[-1,1] \times \mathbb{S}^1 \times \mathbb{S}^1</math> || Torus knots
|-
| <math>\mathbb{S}^1 \times \mathbb{S}^1 \times \mathbb{S}^1</math> || (room not embeddable into <math>\mathbb{R}^3</math>)
|}

In the case of Lissajous knots reflections at the boundaries occur in all of the three cube's dimensions. 
In the second case reflections occur in two dimensions and we have a uniform movement in the third dimension.
The third case is nearly equal to the usual movement on a torus, with an additional triangle wave movement in the first dimension.
